title: Skeletal & Muscular Systems
subtitle: Your body's roll cage, and the engine that moves it.
objectives: Name the five jobs the skeleton does for the body
Locate and name the major bones of the human skeleton
Explain how bone structure protects the body during impact
Describe how exercise and puberty change bone density
Distinguish skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle
Explain how muscles move bones through antagonistic pairs
Explain why daily training now affects bone and muscle health for life

cards.title: Every car you like has a skeleton too
cards.text: Strip the panels off a race car. Underneath is a cage of steel tubes. That cage is why a driver can hit a wall and walk away.

cards.title: You're inside one right now
cards.text: 206 bones. Arranged so the parts that can't heal — brain, heart, lungs, spinal cord — always sit behind something hard.

cards.title: Five jobs, one frame
cards.text: Most people think bones just hold you up. That's one job out of five.
points: **Support** — the frame everything else hangs off.
**Protection** — armour for organs that can't repair themselves.
**Movement** — bones are levers. Muscles pull, bones move.
**Blood and storage** — marrow makes blood cells; bones bank calcium.

cards.title: Tap any bone
cards.text: Each one has a car fact and a boxing fact. Two quiz questions come from this diagram.

cards.title: Death Stranding has this exactly right
cards.text: Sam straps on a Power Skeleton to carry more cargo. That's an exoskeleton — a skeleton worn on the outside.
points: **Yours is an endoskeleton** — on the inside.
**Crabs and beetles** wear theirs outside, like Sam's rig.
**The whole game is load-bearing.** Balance, weight, centre of gravity.

question.text: Sam's Power Skeleton is worn outside his body. What is a skeleton on the outside called?
question.explain: An exoskeleton. Crabs and beetles have them. Yours is an endoskeleton — endo means inside.

cards.title: A seatbelt lands on bone on purpose
cards.text: Engineers routed it across three places: collarbone, ribs, hips. All bone. It avoids your stomach completely.
points: **The lap belt sits on your pelvis**, not your belly.
**Your pelvis can take the hit.** Your intestines cannot.
**Worn too high**, a crash loads soft organs instead of bone.

cards.title: Your clavicle is built to break
cards.text: It's the most commonly fractured bone in your body. That's a feature, not a flaw.
points: **It snaps at a lower force** than your neck or spine.
**Breaking absorbs the energy** before it reaches something worse.
**Same idea as a fuse** blowing to save the wiring.

question.text: Why does a lap belt need to sit low across your hips?
options: So the force lands on your pelvis, not your organs
So it's more comfortable on long drives
So the airbag can reach you faster
question.explain: Your pelvis is one of the strongest structures you own. Worn high, that same force goes into your intestines.

cards.title: Ribs crumple. The skull doesn't.
cards.text: Two body parts, two opposite designs — for the same reason cars are built that way.
points: **Ribs flex and can break.** That absorbs energy. Bone heals.
**The skull doesn't flex at all.** Brains don't heal like bone.
**A car does both**: the front crumples, the cabin stays rigid.

cards.title: One design, a car and a ribcage
cards.text: Orange stays rigid. Blue is meant to deform. Engineers and evolution reached the same answer.

cards.title: The bones that actually hit
cards.text: A punch is force travelling up a chain of bones. The fist is the last link, not the first.
points: **Metacarpals are the striking bones** — the five in your palm.
**Land on the index and middle knuckles.** They're thickest and best braced.
**Power starts at the floor**, not the hand.

cards.title: The punch chain
cards.text: Five links. Miss one and the punch is arm-only.

cards.title: Boxer's fracture is a technique problem
cards.text: It's the 5th metacarpal — the pinky-side one. It breaks when you land a punch turned slightly outward.
points: **Most common hand injury** in combat sports.
**Not a strength problem.** It's about how the fist lands.
**Wraps compress 27 hand bones** into one solid block.

cards.title: Why coaches shout about your chin
cards.text: Your jaw is a lever attached near your brain. A clean shot rotates your skull fast.
points: **Your brain floats in fluid.** It keeps moving after the skull stops.
**That rotation causes the knockout** — not the pain.
**Chin tuck removes the lever.** That's the whole reason for it.

question.text: Tap the bone a seatbelt crosses — the one that's built to break first.
question.explain: The clavicle. It's the most fractured bone in the body, and that's exactly what it's for.

cards.text: Over a quarter of your bones are in your hands. 27 per hand, 54 out of 206. Evolution really committed to grabbing things.

cards.title: How strong are your bones, really?
cards.text: Zack D. Films on what bone can actually take. Loud and fast — then we get back to it.
Forza rates cars on power-to-weight. By that stat bone beats mild steel and concrete. Your femur out-specs the car it's sitting in.

cards.title: Bone is alive and rebuilding
cards.text: Two crews work on your skeleton around the clock. Right now the builders are winning.
points: **Osteoblasts build** new bone tissue.
**Osteoclasts clear away** the old.
**Memory trick:** blasts Build, clasts Crush.

cards.title: You're in the window. It closes.
cards.text: Puberty triggers the fastest bone-building of your life. About 90% of your adult bone mass is set by age 18–20.
points: **After your late twenties** you mostly maintain, then slowly lose.
**You can't redo this window** later.
**What you do now** sets the floor for your seventies.

question.text: Roughly how much of your adult bone mass is locked in by age 18–20?
question.explain: About 90%. It's the biggest bone-building window you get, and it doesn't reopen later.

cards.title: Cyberpunk has a Skeleton slot
cards.text: You install titanium bone lacing to carry more weight and take more damage. That stat is real.
points: **Real bone already does this.** It's called density.
**You can't buy the upgrade** at a ripperdoc.
**Loading your bones is the install.** That's the only way in.

cards.title: Wolff's Law: bone adapts to load
cards.text: Load a bone regularly and your body reinforces it exactly where the stress is.
points: **A boxer's forearms are denser** than average. So are a runner's shins.
**Your training is compounding** into your actual skeleton.
**Growth plates are still cartilage** — that's why coaches cap heavy loads now.

cards.title: Drag the load and watch the bone change
cards.text: This is the inside of a bone. Struts thicken where they're loaded, and vanish where they're not.

cards.title: Pacific Drive is Wolff's Law
cards.text: You bolt armour onto the panels that keep getting wrecked. You reinforce where the damage lands.
points: **Your bones do that automatically.**
**No crafting menu, no scrap.** Just load, and wait.
**Same rule, no inventory.**

cards.text: Astronauts lose 1–2% of bone density every month in orbit. No gravity means no load, so the body stops reinforcing.

question.text: Exercise makes bones denser because bone adapts to the loads placed on it.
question.explain: That's Wolff's Law. Astronauts prove it in reverse — remove the load and density drops fast.

terms.def: The dome of the skull around the brain. Rigid on purpose.
Lower jaw. The only skull bone that moves freely.
Collarbone. The most commonly fractured bone in the body.
Breastbone. The flat plate your ribs attach to.
The 33 stacked bones of the spine. They shield the spinal cord.
Thigh bone. Longest and strongest bone you have.
The five long bones in your palm. You punch with these.
Tissue inside bones that makes blood cells.
The cell that builds new bone.
The cell that breaks down old bone.
Cartilage near the ends of long bones. It's where you grow.
How tightly packed with minerals a bone is.

cards.title: The whole skeletal system, plainly
cards.text: A calm run through bones, ligaments, tendons and cartilage. Good to replay before the exam.

cards.title: Bones — the four that matter
points: **206 bones**, five jobs: support, protect, move, make blood, store minerals.
**Skull rigid, ribs flexible** — because brains don't heal.
**Clavicle breaks first** on purpose, like a fuse.
**Metacarpals strike**; the 5th is the one that breaks.

cards.title: The chassis is done. Install the engine.
cards.text: A bare skeleton can't do anything. It's a frame with no power. This half is the drivetrain.

cards.title: A muscle can only pull
cards.text: It can never push. Every movement you've ever made was something being pulled shorter.
points: **Blinking, walking, throwing a jab** — all pulling.
**So muscles come in opposing pairs.** One pulls it closed, one pulls it open.
**Biceps and triceps** are the textbook example.

question.text: Muscles can only do one thing to a bone. Which is it?
question.explain: Pull, always. That's why every muscle has an opposite that pulls the other way.

cards.title: The three types side by side
cards.text: This is the comparison the exam asks for. Stripes, control, and where each one lives.

cards.title: Skeletal muscle — the one you control
cards.text: Attached to bones. Striped under a microscope. You have over 600 of them.
points: **Voluntary** — you decide when it fires.
**It gets tired.** That's the trade-off for power.
**Everything you can flex on purpose** is this.

cards.title: Smooth muscle — the automatic one
cards.text: In the walls of hollow organs: stomach, intestines, blood vessels, bladder.
points: **Involuntary** — you can't control it.
**Not striped** under a microscope.
**It squeezes food through your gut** whether you think about it or not.

cards.title: Cardiac muscle — the one that never stops
cards.text: Found in exactly one place: your heart. It has its own electrical pacemaker.
points: **Involuntary, but striped** — it borrows from both other types.
**It beats without your brain.** No signal required.
**100,000 beats a day.** No day off, ever.

cards.title: See real muscle tissue
cards.text: The Institute of Human Anatomy, on the three muscle types. Under a minute.

question.text: Which muscle type is found only in the heart and never gets tired?
question.explain: Cardiac muscle. Striped like skeletal, involuntary like smooth, and the only one with its own pacemaker.

cards.title: What 'stay loose' actually means
cards.text: A jab is your triceps extending the elbow. Your biceps does the opposite job.
points: **Tense the biceps mid-punch** and you're fighting yourself.
**Speed comes from the antagonist relaxing** on time.
**A tense arm is slower.** That's mechanics, not mindset.

cards.title: Bend the arm and watch which muscle pulls
cards.text: Tap the button. Notice that the relaxed muscle never pushes — the other one just pulls the opposite way.

cards.title: Tendon or ligament?
cards.text: This is the most confused pair in the whole topic, and the exam knows it.
points: **Tendon** attaches muscle **T**o the bone.
**Ligament** **L**inks two bones together.
**Both are tough.** They just connect different things.

question.text: What connects a muscle to a bone?
question.explain: A tendon. Ligaments link bone to bone — Tendon To the muscle, Ligament Links two bones.

cards.title: You don't grow in the gym
cards.text: Training damages muscle. Recovery builds it. The session is the signal, not the growth.
points: **Hard training tears fibres** microscopically.
**Your body repairs them thicker.** That's hypertrophy.
**It happens while you sleep.** Skip sleep, throw away the session.

cards.text: Your jaw muscle is the strongest in your body for its size. It can push over 90 kg of force through your molars.

terms.def: Voluntary, striped, attached to bones. It tires.
Involuntary, not striped, in hollow organs and vessels.
Involuntary, striped, heart only. Never tires.
You control it consciously.
It runs automatically, without you.
Connects muscle to bone.
Connects bone to bone at a joint.
Two muscles with opposite jobs, like biceps and triceps.
Muscle fibres growing thicker after training and rest.

question.text: Which is built during sleep rather than during the session — muscle, or bone density?
question.explain: Both. Training is the signal for each one. The building happens afterwards, mostly while you sleep.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: Bones and muscles are done. Part 3 is short, and it's the part that's actually about you. Your place is saved either way.

cards.title: Now the part about your daily exercises
cards.text: You train every day. Here's what that's really doing — and it isn't just making you tired.

cards.title: A workout is a message to your bones
cards.text: Load a bone and it sends one signal: reinforce here. Your osteoblasts turn up and add material.
points: **No load, no signal.** Your body won't spend material it doesn't need.
**Daily beats occasional.** Bone answers repeated messages, not one big one.
**You're doing this right now**, whether you notice it or not.

cards.title: Growth hormone, and how to get more of yours
cards.text: Your pituitary gland releases growth hormone in pulses. Two things trigger the big ones.
points: **Deep sleep** produces the largest pulses of your whole day.
**Hard training** triggers another release on top of that.
**Puberty is the peak.** You will never produce more than now.

cards.text: The version in a bottle is a banned drug with real side effects. The version you make while asleep is free, legal and better.

cards.title: Some exercise barely touches bone
cards.text: Bone responds to impact and resistance. Great cardio doesn't automatically mean strong bones.
points: **Running, jumping, lifting, boxing** load bone hard.
**Swimming and cycling** are brilliant for your heart, light on bone.
**Your boxing training is already the bone-building kind.**

question.text: Which of these builds bone density the most?
question.explain: Impact and resistance load bone. Swimming and cycling are excellent cardio, but your bones barely feel them.

cards.title: What happens to people who skip it
cards.text: Bone and muscle both peak, then decline. How steep that fall gets depends on what you built, and what you keep doing.

cards.title: Osteoporosis: bones full of holes
cards.text: Density drops until the inside of a bone looks like a sponge. Then bones break from small falls.
points: **Muscle fades too.** That's sarcopenia, and it starts around 30.
**Weak muscle means more falls.** Weak bone means worse landings.
**A hip fracture at 80** often ends living independently.

cards.title: Death Stranding already showed you this
cards.text: Overload Sam, give him bad balance, and he stumbles and drops everything he's carrying.
points: **That's an untrained old body.** Weak frame, weak stabilisers.
**The game hands you a Power Skeleton.** Real life doesn't.
**You build yours in advance.** There's no shop.

question.text: Growth hormone's biggest release of the day happens while you are in deep sleep.
question.explain: True. Which makes sleep part of training, not a break from it. Skip it and you throw away most of the session.

cards.title: Manny Pacquiao
cards.text: He turned pro at 16, weighing under 110 pounds — too light to make the smallest weight class.
points: **He became the only boxer** to win world titles in eight divisions.
**He was still fighting at world level** in his forties.
**That wasn't luck.** It was decades of daily work.

cards.title: Hidilyn Diaz
cards.text: Stranded abroad during the pandemic with no gym, she trained using water jugs and bamboo poles.
points: **Tokyo 2020:** the first Olympic gold the Philippines ever won.
**No equipment, no excuse.** She loaded whatever she had.
**Weightlifting is bone-loading** in its purest form.

cards.title: Today's session is a deposit
points: **You can't feel bone density changing.** That's why it's easy to skip.
**Every session now** gets stored in your actual skeleton.
**You're building the body** you'll be using at seventy.
**The window is open right now.**

cards.title: Muscles — the four that matter
points: **Three types:** skeletal (you control), smooth (organs), cardiac (heart only).
**Muscles only pull**, so they work in opposing pairs.
**Tendon** = muscle to bone. **Ligament** = bone to bone.
**Muscle is built during sleep**, not during the session.

quiz.text: How many bones are in the adult human skeleton?
quiz.explain: 206 in an adult. You were born with about 270. Many fused together as you grew.
quiz.objective: Name the five jobs the skeleton does for the body

quiz.text: Tap the bone that breaks most often — the one a seatbelt crosses.
quiz.explain: The clavicle. It breaks at a lower force than your neck or spine, so it absorbs the energy first.
quiz.objective: Explain how bone structure protects the body during impact

quiz.text: The skull flexes on impact to absorb energy, the same way ribs do.
quiz.explain: False. Ribs flex and may break, because bone heals. The skull stays rigid, because brain tissue doesn't.
quiz.objective: Explain how bone structure protects the body during impact

quiz.text: A boxer lands a punch turned outward and breaks a hand bone. Which one?
options: The 5th metacarpal, on the pinky side
The humerus, in the upper arm
quiz.explain: The 5th metacarpal — the classic boxer's fracture. Landing rotated loads the weakest striking bone.
quiz.objective: Locate and name the major bones of the human skeleton

quiz.text: Which cell BUILDS new bone tissue?
quiz.explain: Osteoblasts build. Osteoclasts clear away. Blasts Build, Clasts Crush.
quiz.objective: Describe how exercise and puberty change bone density

quiz.text: Put the punch force chain in order, from where power starts to where it lands.
quiz.explain: Power starts at the floor and travels up. That's why coaches fix your feet when a punch feels weak.
quiz.objective: Explain how bone structure protects the body during impact

quiz.text: Roughly how much of your adult bone mass is set by age 18–20?
quiz.explain: About 90%. Puberty is the biggest bone-building window you get, and it doesn't reopen.
quiz.objective: Describe how exercise and puberty change bone density

quiz.text: Tap the longest and strongest bone in your body.
quiz.explain: The femur. It carries several times your bodyweight with every step you take.
quiz.objective: Locate and name the major bones of the human skeleton

quiz.text: Astronauts lose bone density in space because there is no gravity load to adapt to.
quiz.explain: True. Wolff's Law running backwards. No load means no reason to keep the material.
quiz.objective: Describe how exercise and puberty change bone density

quiz.text: Why must a lap belt sit low, across your hips?
options: So the force is carried by the pelvis, not soft organs
So it is more comfortable on long drives
So it does not wrinkle your shirt
So the airbag can reach you faster
quiz.explain: The pelvis can take the load. Worn high, that force goes into your intestines instead.
quiz.objective: Explain how bone structure protects the body during impact

quiz.text: Which muscle type is found only in the heart and never tires?
quiz.explain: Cardiac muscle. It's the only one with a built-in pacemaker, so it beats without the brain.
quiz.objective: Distinguish skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle

quiz.text: A muscle can push as well as pull, depending on what the brain tells it.
quiz.explain: False. Muscles only pull. That's exactly why they come in opposing pairs like biceps and triceps.
quiz.objective: Explain how muscles move bones through antagonistic pairs

quiz.text: Food is squeezed along your intestines automatically. Which muscle does that?
quiz.explain: Smooth muscle. Involuntary, and found in the walls of hollow organs like the gut.
quiz.objective: Distinguish skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle

quiz.text: What tissue attaches MUSCLE to BONE?
quiz.explain: A tendon. Ligaments link bone to bone. Tendon To the muscle, Ligament Links two bones.
quiz.objective: Explain how muscles move bones through antagonistic pairs

quiz.text: You throw a straight punch. Which muscle extends your elbow?
quiz.explain: The triceps. The biceps is its antagonist, which is why tensing it slows the punch down.
quiz.objective: Explain how muscles move bones through antagonistic pairs

quiz.text: Put muscle building in the right order.
quiz.explain: Training is the signal. Recovery is the building. Most of it happens while you sleep.
quiz.objective: Distinguish skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle

quiz.text: Which activity does the most to increase bone density?
quiz.explain: Bone responds to impact and resistance. Swimming and cycling are great cardio but load bone very little.
quiz.objective: Explain why daily training now affects bone and muscle health for life

quiz.text: Your biggest daily release of growth hormone happens during deep sleep.
quiz.explain: True. Sleep is part of training. Hard exercise triggers a second release on top of it.
quiz.objective: Explain why daily training now affects bone and muscle health for life

options: Bone density dropping until bones break easily
Cartilage wearing out in the joints
quiz.explain: Bone loses density until the inside looks like a sponge. The muscle version is called sarcopenia.
quiz.objective: Explain why daily training now affects bone and muscle health for life

teacher.summary: Week 1 Science covers the skeletal system and the muscular system, matching the Term 1 weekly scope. Content is delivered as a card deck with five embedded checkpoints, followed by a 16-item quiz. The format follows the rules in docs/WRITING-FOR-ADHD.md: one idea per card, a 40-word ceiling, and retrieval practice every four to six cards. Part 3 links the biology to his own daily training: what loading does to bone, growth hormone and sleep, the long-term cost of skipping it, and two Filipino athletes as worked examples.
discussion: Ask him to explain the clavicle-as-a-fuse idea in his own words. If he can, he understands energy absorption rather than a bone name.
Ask why the skull and ribs are built differently. 'Because brains don't heal' shows he is reasoning about design trade-offs.
Ask him to name the three muscle types with one location each. This is the most likely exam question format for the week.
Ask what he'd change about his training now that he knows the bone-building window closes. It links biology to a decision he controls.
Ask him which of his own weekly activities actually load bone, and which don't. Getting swimming into the 'low bone load' column shows he's applying the rule rather than reciting it.
teacher.extension: Have him sketch a car's safety cage and label three parts with the bone that does the same job. Five minutes, and it tests transfer rather than recall.
misconceptions: 'Bones are dead.' Bone is living tissue with a blood supply, nerves, and two cell types constantly rebuilding it.
'You lose bones as you grow.' Bones fuse rather than disappear — 270 down to 206.
'Strong bones come from calcium alone.' Calcium is the material. Loading is the signal that tells the body where to put it.
'Muscles push when you straighten your arm.' They don't. The opposing muscle pulls. Pushing is not something muscle can do.
'Tendons and ligaments are the same.' Tendon connects muscle to bone; ligament connects bone to bone.
'All exercise builds bone equally.' Impact and resistance load bone; swimming and cycling do very little for it despite being excellent cardiovascular training.
